auto-mechanic.intro: Learn automotive repair from diagnostics to engine work. One of the most reliable trades in West Africa — the vehicle fleet keeps growing and every one of them breaks down eventually.

skillDomains.name: Workshop Safety
skillDomains.description: The rules that keep you and your customers alive.

skills.name: Workshop Hazards
skills.description: Know the dangers before you turn a wrench.

modules.title: What kills mechanics
modules.content:
Mechanics get hurt by:

  • Falling cars — improper jacking, no jack stands
  • Hot parts — exhaust manifolds, coolant, oil
  • Electrical — battery short circuits, alternator output
  • Fumes — carbon monoxide from running engines in closed spaces
  • Fuel — petrol ignites easily
  • Moving parts — belts, fans, wheels spinning under power

Each of these has killed an experienced mechanic who got careless.

modules.title: Lifting a vehicle safely
modules.content:
Never work under a car held only by a jack

Hydraulic jacks fail. They fail without warning.

The rule

  1. Jack the car at a manufacturer-approved point
  2. Place jack stands under the chassis or axle
  3. Lower the jack slowly onto the stands
  4. Shake the car gently to confirm stability
  5. Only then go under

Wheel chocks on the opposite wheels add another layer of safety.

steps.q: You need to change a tyre. The car is up on a jack only. Can you start?
o: Only if it's a small car
steps.f: Never work under a car supported only by a jack.

steps.q: An engine must run for diagnosis in an enclosed workshop. What do you do?
o: Open the workshop doors or use an exhaust extraction hose
Ignore — it's fine for a minute
steps.f: Carbon monoxide kills without warning.

steps.q: You're removing a battery terminal. Which order?
steps.f: Negative first when disconnecting.

skillDomains.name: Diagnostics
skillDomains.description: Find the fault before replacing parts.

skills.name: Fault Diagnosis
skills.description: Systematic process to find what's actually broken.

modules.title: The diagnostic mindset
modules.content:
Bad mechanics replace parts until the car works. This wastes the customer's money.

The systematic approach

  1. Listen to the customer
  2. Reproduce the fault yourself if possible
  3. Narrow — is it engine, transmission, electrical, brakes, or suspension?
  4. Test — confirm your hypothesis with a measurement
  5. Repair — replace the confirmed faulty part
  6. Verify — confirm the fault is gone

Every step uses evidence, not guessing.

steps.q: Car pulls to one side when braking. Which system?
steps.f: Pulling under braking points to brake imbalance or alignment.

steps.q: Rough idle with a check engine light. Which system?
steps.f: Rough idle almost always traces to fuel delivery or ignition.

steps.q: Whining noise when turning the steering wheel. Which system?
steps.f: Whining on steering points to low power steering fluid or a failing pump.

modules.title: OBD and diagnostic scanners
modules.content:
Modern cars (1996+) have an On-Board Diagnostics (OBD) port. A scanner reads the fault codes the car's computer stores.

What codes tell you

  • A P0301 code means cylinder 1 misfire
  • A P0420 code means catalyst efficiency below threshold

What codes don't tell you

The code tells you the symptom, not the cause. P0301 could be a bad spark plug, bad coil, bad injector, or wiring.

Every mechanic today should own or have access to an OBD scanner.

skillDomains.name: Engine Systems
skillDomains.description: The core of the vehicle. Understand how combustion, lubrication, and cooling work together.

skills.name: Four-Stroke Cycle
skills.description: The fundamental engine cycle every mechanic must know cold.

modules.title: Intake, compression, power, exhaust
modules.content:
1. Intake — piston moves down, intake valve opens, fuel-air mixture enters
  2. Compression — piston moves up, both valves closed, mixture compresses
  3. Power — spark plug ignites the mixture (petrol), explosion pushes piston down
  4. Exhaust — piston moves up, exhaust valve opens, gases leave

Diesel engines ignite by compression heat instead of a spark plug — everything else is the same.

steps.q: Which stroke produces power?
steps.f: The power stroke is where ignition drives the piston down.

steps.q: In a four-cylinder engine, how many cylinders are firing per revolution?
steps.f: One cylinder fires per revolution in a four-cylinder four-stroke engine.

steps.q: Diesel engines differ from petrol engines mainly in:
steps.f: Diesel ignites by compression heat; petrol needs a spark.

skills.name: Cooling System
skills.description: Overheating destroys engines. Understand how to prevent it.

modules.title: Why engines need cooling
modules.content:
Combustion temperatures exceed 2,000°C. Without cooling, the engine destroys itself in minutes.

The cooling loop

  1. Coolant flows through passages in the engine block
  2. Absorbs heat
  3. Flows to the radiator
  4. Airflow through the radiator cools the coolant
  5. Coolant returns to the engine
  6. A thermostat regulates the flow

Common failures

  • Low coolant (leak)
  • Failed thermostat
  • Failed water pump
  • Blocked radiator
  • Failed cooling fan

steps.q: Temperature gauge climbs in traffic but drops at highway speed. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Highway speed forces air through; traffic relies on the fan.

steps.q: Coolant is disappearing but there's no visible leak. What do you check?
steps.f: Hidden coolant loss usually means a head gasket leak.

steps.q: Engine overheats immediately after starting cold. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Immediate overheat means coolant isn't circulating.

modules.title: Perform a cooling system service
modules.prompt: Document the steps to drain, flush, and refill a cooling system on any vehicle you have access to.
steps: Locate the drain plug and radiator cap
Drain old coolant into a proper container
Flush with clean water until it runs clear
Run engine with heater on, top off, check for leaks

skillDomains.name: Automotive Electrical
skillDomains.description: Modern cars are computers on wheels. Electrical knowledge is a mechanic's edge.

skills.name: Battery & Charging
skills.description: The 12V system that starts and runs everything.

modules.title: The 12V system
modules.content:
Almost all cars run a 12V electrical system.

The key components

  • Battery — stores energy for starting
  • Alternator — charges the battery while the engine runs
  • Starter motor — cranks the engine
  • Fuses and relays — protect circuits

Voltage checks

  • Engine off, battery should read 12.4-12.7V
  • Engine running, alternator should produce 13.8-14.4V
  • Below 12V off = battery failing
  • Below 13.5V running = alternator failing

steps.q: Battery reads 12.0V with engine off. What does this mean?
o: About 50% discharged — needs charging or replacement
steps.f: 12.0V is roughly half discharged.

steps.q: Engine running, battery reads 12.5V. What's the problem?
o: Alternator is not charging — should be 13.8-14.4V
steps.f: If voltage doesn't rise above 13.8V with engine running, the alternator or belt is failing.

steps.q: Battery keeps going flat overnight. What do you check first?
steps.f: A parasitic drain pulls power even with the key off.

skills.name: Starting System
skills.description: What happens when you turn the key.

modules.title: The starting chain
modules.content:
Turning the key triggers a chain of events:

  1. Battery sends current to the starter solenoid
  2. Solenoid engages the starter gear with the flywheel
  3. Starter motor spins the engine
  4. Engine fires and runs
  5. Solenoid disengages the starter

Common failures

  • Click but no crank — solenoid or starter failing
  • Slow crank — weak battery or bad connections
  • No sound at all — ignition switch, relay, or wiring
  • Crank but no start — fuel or ignition problem

steps.q: Turn key, hear a single loud click, engine doesn't crank. Most likely?
steps.f: A click means the solenoid engages but the starter doesn't spin.

steps.q: Engine cranks slowly, especially when cold. What do you check first?
o: Battery state of charge and terminal condition
steps.f: Slow crank in cold = weak battery or corroded terminals.

steps.q: Engine cranks fast but doesn't start. What's the problem?
steps.f: Cranking is fine — the problem is downstream.

skillDomains.name: Brakes & Suspension
skillDomains.description: The systems that keep the car safe on the road.

skills.name: Brake Systems
skills.description: The most safety-critical system on any vehicle.

modules.title: How brakes work
modules.content:
When you press the brake pedal:

  1. Pedal pushes hydraulic fluid through lines
  2. Fluid pressure reaches the wheel cylinders or calipers
  3. Pads or shoes press against the rotating disc or drum
  4. Friction slows the wheel

Two types

  • Disc brakes — pads squeeze a rotating disc
  • Drum brakes — shoes press against an inner drum

Brake fluid

Brake fluid absorbs water over time, which lowers its boiling point. Flush every 2 years.

steps.q: Squealing noise when braking. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Squealing under braking usually means pads have worn down to the wear indicator.

steps.q: Brake pedal feels soft or spongy. What do you check?
o: Brake fluid level and possible air in the lines
steps.f: A soft pedal means fluid loss or air in the system.

steps.q: Car pulls to one side under braking. What causes this?
o: Seized caliper or contaminated pads on one side
steps.f: Uneven braking means one side works harder.

skills.name: Suspension
skills.description: Ride, handling, and safety depend on it.

modules.title: What suspension does
modules.content:
Suspension keeps the wheels on the road while the body absorbs bumps.

Key components

  • Springs — support the weight, absorb bumps
  • Shock absorbers / struts — control the springs, prevent bouncing
  • Control arms — connect wheels to the frame
  • Bushings — cushion the joints
  • Sway bars — reduce body roll in corners

Signs of worn suspension

  • Car bounces after bumps
  • Uneven tyre wear
  • Nose dives under braking
  • Clunking over bumps

steps.q: Car keeps bouncing after a bump. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Bouncing after the bump means shocks aren't controlling the springs.

steps.q: Clunking noise over bumps. What do you check?
o: Worn bushings or loose suspension components
steps.f: Clunking points to worn bushings, ball joints, or sway bar links.

steps.q: Front tyres wear unevenly on the inside edge. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Inner edge wear usually means negative camber or incorrect toe.

skills.name: Estimating & Billing
skills.description: Quote jobs correctly so the workshop survives.

modules.title: How a workshop makes money
modules.content:
Three revenue streams

  1. Parts — the markup on replacement parts
  2. Labour — the hourly rate for time
  3. Services — oil changes, diagnostics, tune-ups

Parts markup

Workshops typically mark up parts 20-50%.

Labour rate

Set a labour rate that covers overhead and profit.

The rule

Never quote a job without inspecting first. Customers describe symptoms; you find the cause.

skills.name: Customer Trust
skills.description: In this trade, reputation is everything.

modules.title: Why trust matters more in mechanics
modules.content:
Customers can't see what you do. They have to trust you. This makes reputation the single most valuable asset a mechanic owns.

How trust is built

  • Show the customer the failed part
  • Explain what you found and why it needs replacing
  • Never replace a part that doesn't need replacing
  • Give a warranty on your work
  • Stand by your repairs
  • Charge fairly and transparently

How trust is destroyed

  • Charging for work you didn't do
  • Replacing parts that were fine
  • Blame-shifting on comeback jobs
  • Disappearing after a bad job

modules.title: Build a service record system
modules.prompt: Design a system for tracking every customer vehicle and its service history.
steps: Choose a method (paper card, notebook, spreadsheet)
Include fields: vehicle reg, owner, date, work done, parts used, cost
Add a reminder field for next service
Test it on 5 real or imagined vehicles
Refine based on how easy it is to use
